title: Repaying parents
hookLine: a hundred years on your shoulders isn't enough: two Buddhist answers to what repays a parent
tomorrow: and when a parent is hard to be around?

cards: What could ever repay a parent? Rides, meals, nights up with a fever, small worries kept quiet. People try: a card, a trip, a new couch for the living room.
The Buddha's answer starts with an image that sounds like a challenge. Carry your mother on one shoulder and your father on the other, for a hundred years. It still wouldn't be enough.

teach.h: ONE VOICE: HELP THEM TO GOODNESS.
teach.b: Bathe them, feed them, even make them rulers of the whole earth: still not repaid. Because parents do so much for their children; they raise them, feed them, show them the world.
Then comes the one repayment the Buddha does name. If they lack faith, help them to faith. If they lack virtue, help them to virtue.
Stingy, to generosity. Unwise, to wisdom. That repays, and more.
Now two voices from inside the tradition. The first stands on this sutta. Carrying parents is love, but it gives them nothing that lasts.
Only goodness lasts, so the real gift is helping them toward it, gently, by example as much as by words. The second voice comes from the Ullambana Sutra, read in East Asian and Vietnamese Buddhism.
There the monk Moggallana sees his dead mother suffering and can't reach her himself. The Buddha tells him to make offerings to the whole community of monks, and the merit frees her.
From that story comes Vu Lan, a festival for parents living and gone; at some Vietnamese temples people pin on a rose, red if their mother is living, white if she has died.
This voice says: not every parent will listen to a child.
Offerings made in their name reach them anyway, even after death.

teach.h: VU LAN, A ROSE, RED OR WHITE.
teach.b: Both voices agree on one thing.
Service alone can't repay. Goodness, shared, is the only coin that counts.

how: Some Theravada Buddhists honor parents by making merit in their name; in Vietnamese, Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, the Vu Lan or Ullambana festival is a time of offerings for parents and ancestors.

o: a debt to parents that care alone can't settle
a vow to live with your parents until they die
a fixed share of income owed to parents for life

games.q: two ways to repay — tap the pairs.
p: a hundred years on your shoulders
help them to faith, virtue, giving, wisdom
a white rose at Vu Lan
for a mother who has died

s: in the sutta, enough years of caring for parents finally repays them
even a hundred years carrying them, even making them rulers, doesn't. only helping them toward goodness does.
in the Ullambana Sutra, Moggallana's mother is freed through offerings to the community of monks
he couldn't reach her himself; the merit of the offering did.
Buddhism teaches that children owe their parents nothing, because of karma
the sutta calls parents hard to repay, and names how to repay them.

games.q: your friend's family celebrates Vu Lan with offerings for their parents and grandparents. you lean toward the sutta's view: help them to goodness yourself. what's the best case for their way?
o: offerings are easier than trying to change anyone's mind.
not every parent will listen; offerings in their name reach them anyway, even after death.
the Buddha said only offerings repay parents, not anything a child says.
games.why: the Ullambana tradition's strongest case: Moggallana couldn't reach his mother, and the merit of the offering did. both voices agree service alone can't repay.

practice: Count on your fingers, slowly, things a parent or whoever raised you did that you didn't notice at the time: a ride, a meal, a worry kept quiet. Give each one a breath of thanks.
If the people who raised you were hard to be around, count whoever else carried you; the sutta's point holds for them too.

wordCard.voice: Repaying parents: a debt service can't settle. One voice repays with goodness shared, face to face; another, with offerings made in their name, here or after they're gone.

orig.note: Pali: grateful, knowing what was done for you; the quality behind repaying parents.

carryVoice: Worth holding: hard to repay, and goodness is the only coin that counts. Two of eleven, on family.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 2.32 (Kataññu Sutta; 2.33 in some numberings: carrying mother and father on one's shoulders for a hundred years, bathing them, making them rulers, would not repay them; encouraging them to faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom repays and more than repays)
Ullambana Sutra (Moggallana/Maudgalyayana sees his mother among hungry ghosts and, on the Buddha's instruction, makes offerings to the sangha at the end of the rains retreat to free her)
